{{DISPLAYTITLE:Computation inside proofs}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Definitional equality|Lean theorem prover/System/Decision procedures}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Some statements are proved by calculating. That 2 + 2 is 4, or that 97 is prime, can be
settled by working the sum or by trying every divisor. Lean accepts such calculations as
proofs. This page shows how, what has to be trusted when it does, and what the calculation
costs.

== A sum as a proof ==

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl

example : 2 ^ 100 = 1267650600228229401496703205376 := rfl
</pre>

The proof <code>rfl</code> says that the two sides are the same thing. To accept it, Lean
works out both sides and compares the results. Two expressions that compute to the same value
are, in Lean's terms, '''definitionally equal''', and for them <code>rfl</code> is a complete
proof (see [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Two kinds of equality|two kinds of
equality]]).

The second line raises 2 to the power 100 and is accepted at once. In the logic a natural
number is zero followed by a chain of successors, and a chain of that length could never be
written out. The Lean kernel does not try. It stores number literals in a fast library for
arithmetic on large numbers, usually GMP, and replaces addition, multiplication and the other
basic operations with routines from that library. The Lean Language Reference adds the
condition that comes with the speed: these routines are part of the Lean kernel, so if they
did not agree with the definitions they stand in for, soundness could suffer.<ref name="ref-nat">''The
Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), section 20.1,
"Natural Numbers", with section 20.1.2, "Run-Time Representation".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/</ref>

== Deciding a finite question ==

A finite question can be answered by a program, and the run of the program can be a proof.
Here is a test for primality by trial division, applied to 97:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def isPrime (n : Nat) : Bool :=
  n ≥ 2 &amp;&amp; (List.range (n - 2)).all (fun k => n % (k + 2) != 0)

#eval isPrime 97

theorem prime97 : isPrime 97 = true := by decide

#print axioms prime97
</pre>

The function checks that n is at least 2 and that no number from 2 to n − 1 divides it.
<code>#eval</code> runs it and prints <code>true</code>. That is a program's answer, not yet
a proof. The theorem turns it into one. The tactic <code>decide</code> finds a procedure that
decides the statement and evaluates it inside the logic; when the result is "true", that
evaluation is the proof, and the Lean kernel repeats it when it checks the
theorem.<ref name="ref-tacref">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), section 14.5, "Tactic Reference": entries for <code>decide</code> and
<code>native_decide</code>.
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/</ref> The last
line confirms that nothing extra was assumed: <code>'prime97' does not depend on any
axioms</code>.

== Running the program instead: native_decide ==

The same question can be answered faster by running the program as a program and accepting
its answer:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem prime97_native : isPrime 97 = true := by native_decide

#print axioms prime97_native
#print prime97_native._native.native_decide.ax_1_1
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 answers:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
'prime97_native' depends on axioms: [prime97_native._native.native_decide.ax_1_1]
axiom prime97_native._native.native_decide.ax_1_1 : decide (isPrime 97 = true) = true
</pre>

The theorem now rests on an axiom made for the occasion. <code>native_decide</code> evaluated
the question the way <code>#eval</code> does, and then added an axiom stating the answer. The
Lean kernel asks for no proof of an axiom; it accepts it. So the theorem is only as sound as the
evaluation behind the axiom, which means the Lean compiler and every function that has been
given a faster implementation for running. The reference manual says that this adds the
entire Lean compiler to the trusted part of the system, and that a new axiom will show up in
<code>#print axioms</code> for the theorem and for anything that depends on
it.<ref name="ref-tacref" /> In versions of Lean up to 4.28, such theorems were marked
instead by one shared axiom, <code>Lean.trustCompiler</code>.<ref name="ref-validating">''The
Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), "Validating a Lean
Proof", with the note "On Lean.trustCompiler (up to Lean 4.28.0)".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/</ref>

That is a widening of what must be trusted, not a mistake in the answer. The prime is still
prime. But a reader who wants to rely on the theorem must now trust a much larger body of
code than the Lean kernel. The project this wiki records forbids
<code>native_decide</code> in its own sources, as its proof gate states (see
[[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the transition page]]). Nothing is hidden either way: the
axiom's name appears in the list, as on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What has to be trusted|what has to be trusted]].

== What the calculation costs ==

Evaluation inside the logic is slow. It proceeds step by step through the definitions, with
few of the shortcuts of a compiled program, and it has limits on how deep it may go. Asking
the same question about 1009 shows the difference:

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#eval isPrime 1009

example : isPrime 1009 = true := by decide
</pre>

<code>#eval</code> prints <code>true</code> at once, but <code>decide</code> stops with
<code>maximum recursion depth has been reached</code>. The option <code>decide +kernel</code>
hands the evaluation directly to the Lean kernel, which evaluates the procedure once instead
of twice:<ref name="ref-tacref" />

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem prime1009 : isPrime 1009 = true := by decide +kernel

#print axioms prime1009
</pre>

This succeeds, and <code>'prime1009' does not depend on any axioms</code>. The cost grows with
the size of the question. In one measurement made for this page, on one computer, checking
the same theorem for the six-digit prime 100003 with <code>decide +kernel</code> took about
fifteen seconds, while running the program with <code>#eval</code> took well under a second.
Other computers will give other times.

Some procedures cannot be evaluated inside the logic at all. A decision procedure defined by
well-founded recursion may get stuck, because evaluating it would require working through
proofs as well as data.<ref name="ref-tacref" /> The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Functions that always finish|functions that always finish]]
explains where such definitions come from.

== The choice ==

Computing inside a proof is a trade between speed and trust. Evaluation by the Lean kernel is
slow and bounded, but it adds nothing to what must be trusted. Evaluation by the compiler is
fast, but it adds the compiler, and an axiom, to the foundation of the theorem. When a
calculation is too large for the first, the alternatives include proving a general
theorem that makes the calculation unnecessary, and accepting the larger trust and recording it.
Lean makes the choice visible, so that a reader can see which was taken.
